The stock will trade under the ticker "ANT" after the company raised $81.3 billion in the IPO. The Claude creator sold 980 million shares at $83 a piece on Wednesday, lifting the size and price of its offering. The 5-year-old company captivated the corporate world with its Claude AI models and products, which have fueled its meteoric rise this year. Anthropic said in its prospectus that it generated $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up a staggering 1,200% from the same period last year. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the company in 2021 after he and a small group of researchers defected from OpenAI , now its chief rival. Anthropic has faced sharp criticism over its positions on safety, regulation and national security, including by President Donald Trump and other senior government officials. headlines.article_text: Walmart (WMT) Q3 2026 earnings Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Walmart narrowly topped fiscal third-quarter earnings and revenue estimates and raised its full-year sales and earnings outlook. In an exclusive interview with CNBC, CEO John Furner said Walmart has been working to keep prices low despite soaring diesel costs. The company highlighted e-commerce sales growth as it said it saw success with store-fulfilled pickup and delivery. In this article WMT Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 6:49 06:49 Walmart CEO John Furner on Q3 results: Customers continue to look for value Squawk Box Walmart on Thursday reported earnings and revenue that narrowly topped estimates and raised its full-year outlook as it saw strong e-commerce growth ahead of the busy holiday season. Walmart said global e-commerce sales surged 17% in the fiscal third quarter, driven by store-fulfilled pickup and delivery, with Walmart U.S. up 23% and Sam's Club U.S. rising 30%. Its Walmart U.S. advertising business saw a 37% sales increase for the quarter. Walmart said it rolled back prices on nearly 8,000 products across its stores, a focus as U.S. consumers worry about the cost of living in the face of elevated food and gas prices. CEO John Furner told CNBC's Becky Quick that the company has seen higher-than-expected diesel costs, but that tariff refunds have helped the retailer to offset those inputs and maintain lower prices. "The reality is that increases in diesel fuel and transportation, they do work their way into cost of goods," Furner said in an exclusive interview. "So we're hoping to see these costs come down as soon as possible, and we'll keep prices as low as we can." CFO John David Rainey told CNBC that growth in online orders for Walmart and Sam's Club was driven by an emphasis on speed of delivery and reduced prices. He added that Walmart saw its largest share gains in the food category in three years during the third quarter. "This was another really solid quarter for us, we feel good about it," Rainey told CNBC. "We continue to gain share while continuing to improve the profitability of our digital businesses." Shoppers enter a Walmart store in Charlotte, North Carolina, Aug. 30, 2026. Travis Dove | Bloomberg | Getty Images Walmart also raised its full-year guidance, now expecting net sales to increase between 4.9% and 5.2%, compared with previous guidance of a 4% to 5% increase. Rainey said Walmart is maintaining "flexibility" in its guidance. Walmart anticipates adjusted earnings per share will come in between $2.84 and $2.89, compared with a prior range of $2.80 to $2.87. It's also now expecting adjusted operating income to increase between 8% and 8.6%, up from the previous outlook of between 7% and 8.5% growth. Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: 65 cents adjusted vs. 64 cents expected Revenue: $188.84 billion vs. $187.27 billion expected For the quarter ended Oct. 31, the company reported net income of $4.95 billion, or 62 cents per share, down from $6.14 billion, or 77 cents per share, a year earlier. Revenue rose 5.2%. Adjusting for investment gains and losses, tax matters and reorganization charges, Walmart earned 65 cents per share. Walmart U.S. recorded net sales of $125 billion, up 3.6% from a year earlier. Its comparable sales excluding fuel rose 2.9%, in line with Wall Street expectations, according to StreetAccount. Furner also said Walmart is seeing encouraging adoption of its artificial intelligence agent, named Sparky, especially ahead of the holiday season. He said it's led to customer basket increases of 40% on average. "It just is a great way of just completing the entire basket and solving entire the solution for people," he said. Sam's Club reported net sales of $25.9 billion, marking a 10% increase from the year-ago period. It said its sales were driven by strength in the grocery category and general merchandise. In October, Walmart announced it was launching a joint membership option with Walmart+ and Sam's Club as it leans further into convenience. Both stores will still offer stand-alone memberships, as well. Furner told CNBC the new membership has brought roughly 2 million new people into Sam's Club since its launch in late October. Though the company reimbursed some members for the new membership rate, Rainey added that it's already seeing positive returns on the joint model and that consumers are "spending appreciably more." The company on Thursday said its global membership fee revenue grew 17% in the third quarter. The company is typically well insulated from macroeconomic pressures because of its value reputation. Last quarter , the company said it was lowering prices of products across multiple categories, including beef. Rainey said Thursday that he's "optimistic" about consumer spending heading into the holiday season and that the fourth quarter is already "off to a pretty good start." The big-box retailer has posted solid growth over the past few quarters as it sees customers gravitate to reduced prices, improvements in delivery and gains in its advertising business. It's also leaned into attracting higher-income consumers with its Walmart+ membership. Shares of Walmart have fluctuated this year but are up roughly 13% year to date. headlines.title: Trump bought Nvidia, Palantir, SpaceX in September as federal deals, White House ties grew
headlines.summary: President Trump disclosed purchases of Nvidia stock, SpaceX debt and Tesla shares in September, alongside millions of dollars in other investments.
headlines.article_text: Trump bought Nvidia, Palantir, SpaceX amid federal contracts Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points President Donald Trump's latest financial disclosure reveals 751 September trades worth between $40.9 million and $148.1 million, according to a CNBC analysis of the report. His accounts bought Palantir shares before $42.5 million in federal contract awards and invested in SpaceX around the time of a $946 million NASA contract expansion. Trump's accounts also bought Nvidia shares as then-CEO Jensen Huang strengthened his White House ties. The White House says Trump has no role in managing his investments. In this article NVDA TSLA PLTR Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT President Donald Trump attends a multilateral meeting with delegations from Japan, India and Australia at the Solaire Hotel in Manila, Philippines, Nov. 17, 2026. Win McNamee | Getty Images President Donald Trump's investment accounts bought shares of Nvidia , Palantir and Elon Musk 's SpaceX in September, around the time the companies secured major federal contracts and their executives met with the president, according to a newly released financial disclosure. The 25-page filing shows 751 purchases and sales totaling between roughly $40.9 million and $148.1 million, according to a CNBC analysis. Purchases accounted for at least $29.2 million and sales at least $11.7 million. The filing reports transactions in broad dollar ranges, leaving the exact amounts and value of Trump's holdings unclear. Among the transactions were Palantir purchases before the company received two federal contracts worth $42.5 million combined, according to contracting records, SpaceX investments shortly before and after a $946 million NASA contract expansion , and Nvidia trades as its then-CEO, Jensen Huang , cultivated a close relationship with Trump . The trades underscore a striking feature of Trump's presidency: His personal fortune remains invested in companies whose fortunes his administration can shape. His accounts reported more than 21,000 trades in 2025 , compared with roughly 500 during his entire first term. Recent presidents have generally divested individual stocks or used blind trusts to avoid potential conflicts. The White House has told CNBC previously Trump and his family have no control over the trades, which outside financial managers handle independently . The Trump Organization says the arrangement is designed to avoid even the appearance of a conflict. There is no evidence Trump directed the transactions or that his managers knew government decisions in advance. White House spokesman Davis Ingle said that Trump's portfolio is independently managed and that neither the president nor his family has any input on trades. "All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers," Ingle told CNBC. The Trump Organization did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Read more on Trump investments Trump bought up to $25 million in Meta and millions in SpaceX debt in August Trump’s municipal bond portfolio reaches as much as $1 billion as policy overlaps mount Trump disclosure shows 1,100 July trades, Microsoft and Amazon sales Trump’s oil investments have gained millions during Iran war as his accounts keep trading Trump’s foreign licensing business booms to $59.5 million as Gulf developers pay JPMorgan, Schwab and UBS manage millions in Trump’s $858 million investment portfolio Trump bought as much as $5 million in Axon stock before ICE sought $220 million Taser deal Company that bet big on Trump-backed crypto says its fortunes have improved Trump family got about $500M from crypto venture — but investors saw steep losses Trump Jr. calls banking a 'Ponzi scheme' that forced family to create crypto business The Trump family crypto empire looks to Asia: Eric Trump talks Bitcoin in Hong Kong Trump family says U.S. dollar needs an upgrade and they are the ones to do it The timing was particularly notable at Palantir, the artificial intelligence software maker whose technology is used by U.S. military, intelligence and civilian agencies. Trump's accounts bought between $15,001 and $50,000 in Palantir shares on Sept. 2, followed by another purchase of between $1,001 and $15,000 on Sept. 9. A week later, the Department of Housing and Urban Development awarded Palantir a contract with $10.4 million in initial obligations for AI-powered grant oversight and fraud detection. On Sept. 29, the Department of Homeland Security awarded Palantir another $32.1 million software contract , bringing the two awards to roughly $42.5 million. That same day, CEO Alex Karp joined Trump, Musk, Huang and other technology executives at the White House for a meeting on artificial intelligence . Trump's accounts also bought shares and debt in SpaceX in the weeks surrounding a major NASA contract award. On Sept. 1, the accounts purchased between $100,001 and $250,000 in SpaceX debt carrying a 5.35% interest rate. Eight days later, they bought between $1,001 and $15,000 in shares of the major NASA and Pentagon contractor. On Sept. 18, NASA announced a $946 million expansion of its SpaceX contract, adding three astronaut missions to the International Space Station and bringing the agreement's total value to $5.92 billion. The agency had signaled plans for additional missions in May. Six days after the announcement, Trump's accounts bought another $15,001 to $50,000 in SpaceX shares on the same day Musk attended Trump's White House state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping . The filing does not show whether the purchase came before or after the dinner. The trades followed an even larger SpaceX investment in August , when Trump's accounts bought between $1 million and $5 million in the company's debt just two days before he signed a policy aimed at expanding commercial space transportation. Trump's accounts also continued buying Nvidia shares as Huang drew closer to the president — a relationship now under congressional scrutiny over Huang's ties to a woman suspected of spying for China. The September filing shows four Nvidia purchases totaling between $152,004 and $380,000, including two on Sept. 2 worth as much as $350,000 combined. The accounts also sold between $1,001 and $15,000 in Nvidia shares on Sept. 24, the day Huang also attended the state dinner with Xi. The trades bring Trump's Nvidia transactions to at least 108 since his return to office in 2025, worth between $27.2 million and $97.9 million, extending a CNBC analysis published Monday . The relationship between the president and Nvidia's then-CEO has drawn fresh scrutiny after The New York Times reported that intelligence officials warned Trump about Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Trump has denied being briefed. Huang resigned Nov. 12 following revelations about his personal relationships. The September filing also shows substantial trading beyond the three companies. The largest reported transaction was a Sept. 23 purchase of between $5 million and $25 million in Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF shares. That same day, Trump's accounts sold between $1 million and $5 million each in Comcast , McDonald's , Home Depot and Fidelity National Information Services , along with between $500,001 and $1 million each in Nike and Constellation Brands . On the buy side, Trump's accounts purchased between $250,001 and $500,000 in TJX shares on each of two consecutive days, Sept. 15 and 16. They also bought between $117,004 and $330,000 in Tesla shares across four transactions, along with smaller investments in CoreWeave , Intel , Microsoft and Apple . headlines.article_text: Amazon launches in-app push against New York City delivery bill Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Amazon is showing pop-up notices to some users of its app and website warning against a New York City bill that aims to disrupt its contracted delivery model. A banner on its homepage states the bill, dubbed the Delivery Protection Act, "could add up to $5 per order." Amazon has lobbied heavily against the proposed legislation, while New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani backed the bill earlier this year. In this article AMZN Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT An Amazon driver loads packages into a delivery van at an Amazon delivery station in Alpharetta, Georgia, Nov. 28, 2022. Justin Sullivan | Getty Images Amazon is taking its fight against a New York City delivery bill, which has been backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani , to its shopping website and app. Some users who open the company's shopping app or website report being served with pop-ups and banners warning that the New York City Council "could add up to $5 per order" if it passes Intro 518, or the Delivery Protection Act. The bill would require Amazon to employ its army of third-party delivery companies directly, disrupting the contractor model it has relied on since 2018. Amazon uses a network of thousands of small companies, which often work solely for Amazon, to handle the last-mile portion of shipments, in an effort to speed up deliveries and control more of its logistics operations. "If this legislation passes, we'd no longer be able to work with them, and we'd be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city," Amazon's in-app message states. "That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees." The proposed legislation was introduced in February and is awaiting review by City Council Speaker Julie Menin. Amazon also posted a statement on its company website where it often publishes its policy positions . But rarely has the company used its valuable e-commerce site and app real estate to push its perspectives. Other tech companies including Uber and Lyft have similarly used their apps to advocate for or against legislation in the past. Amazon's pop-up notices and a stationary banner on its store homepage direct users to a form where they can "contact your council member to oppose Intro 518." According to Amazon, 20,000 customers sent emails to city council members in the first six hours that the pop-up appeared. Menin told CNBC in a statement that Amazon's claim it will need to raise prices due to the proposed legislation "defies logic." "We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs," Menin said. "If Amazon thinks this deceptive campaign will effectively threaten New Yorkers and intimidate this City Council, they are dead wrong." Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a statement that the company put up the notices to be "transparent with our customers" about what the bill "would cause them if it passes as written." "If customers are concerned, one of the most impactful things they can do is contact their City Council member and ask them to oppose this bill," Nantel said. The Delivery Protection Act has received a swell of support from labor groups, including the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, which has sought to unionize Amazon delivery and warehouse workers. Hunterbrook disclosed that it had taken a short position in AMD. The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers." CNBC did not independently verify this information. Hunterbrook also said that new export rules in Washington could "tighten restrictions on AMD's foreign business," alleging that AMD "bills over 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong," and "depends on a Chinese partner to finish most of its chips." AMD, 1-day The allegations come amid investigations of rival chipmaker Nvidia over its sales to companies in Asia with ties to China. AMD has been viewed as a beneficiary of the uncertainty surrounding Nvidia. "The claims misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships," an AMD spokesperson said in a statement. "AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations. We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity." Lisa Su, CEO of AMD, told investors on the company's recent earnings call that China is an "important" market and that the semiconductor giant wants to be fully compliant with U.S. export controls.
